content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published evidence on tools for the detection and prevention of leprosy. WHO plans to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of this evidence following its established procedures for issuing new guidelines on leprosy. After this assessment, WHO will determine whether any of the existing tools can be recommended for integration into routine national policies. In the meantime, research on prevention will be encouraged to identify new treatment regimens, develop innovative diagnostic tools, and establish methods for implementing these tools in real-world settings. Globally, the recommended actions include: 1. Reviewing existing tools for prevention and disease management in accordance with WHO's rules and regulations for guideline issuance. 2. Promoting operational research in the areas of prevention and diagnostic testing for infection and disease. In all settings, the recommended actions are: 1. Prioritizing implementation research studies on the use of tools to prevent leprosy and promoting studies on new diagnostic tests to detect infection and disease. 2. Using the outcomes of published research to guide implementation research projects, enabling effective monitoring of the impact of preventive activities. Leprosy-related stigma and discrimination are widespread across nearly all cultures globally. Historically, many societies endorsed stigma through laws enforcing compulsory segregation, which were repealed only in recent decades. Leprosy is often perceived as a punishment for sin, misbehavior, or breaking a taboo. Despite the disease being identified as caused by a germ since 1873, these beliefs persist in many communities. Some countries still have discriminatory laws, such as those allowing divorce or deportation of migrant workers due to leprosy, perpetuating stigma and discrimination. Affected individuals, being part of their communities, are aware of the prevailing negative attitudes and stereotypes about leprosy. This often leads to internalized stigma or self-stigma, where individuals isolate themselves from their communities. Internalized stigma can be as disabling as external stigma and may persist even after overt discrimination has ceased. Stigma and discrimination also extend to family members, creating a family curse with negative social consequences for the entire family. This can affect mental health, leading to increased anxiety, depression, and even suicide attempts. Stigma also impacts social participation, work performance, earning potential, relationships, education opportunities, and access to healthcare. Family members may face reduced opportunities, such as children being denied schooling or siblings struggling to marry. Stigma delays diagnosis, affects treatment compliance, and hinders the implementation of disability prevention activities like self-care. Promoting societal inclusion of individuals affected by leprosy and their families requires raising awareness of the problem and incorporating evidence-based strategies into national leprosy programs and NGO initiatives. Key strategies include addressing stigma and discrimination, empowering affected individuals, involving them in leprosy services, building coalitions with community-based organizations, and ensuring access to social and financial support systems. Stigma can manifest as enacted stigma, leading to discrimination, which may be interpersonal (e.g., job loss or family exclusion) or structural (e.g., policies requiring disclosure of leprosy status on immigration forms or laws allowing divorce due to leprosy). Structural discrimination can also occur in healthcare services, such as limiting leprosy outpatient clinics to specific days, which isolates affected individuals. Research on stigma and discrimination in healthcare and social services is limited, and tools are needed to assess and address these issues. Negative language and stereotypes contribute to stigma. Terms like leper or deformity should be avoided, and positive, dignified language should be encouraged, especially in media and healthcare. Religious leaders play a crucial role in spreading awareness that leprosy is curable and advocating against discrimination. Counseling, empowerment activities, and awareness of human rights can mitigate the impact of stigma, including internalized stigma. Peer counseling, where affected individuals are trained in basic counseling skills, has been effective in countries like Nepal and Indonesia. Socioeconomic development (SED) activities, such as micro-credit loans and business training, empower individuals and reduce stigma. These activities restore individuals' roles in their families and communities, enhancing self-worth and dignity. However, self-employment is not suitable for everyone, so other empowerment strategies, such as training in personal effectiveness and human rights, are also needed. Globally and regionally, actions include promoting awareness and compliance with the UN Human Rights Council Resolution 29/5 (2015), identifying partners to support stigma-reduction strategies, and collecting data on stigma and discrimination to monitor the impact of interventions. Nationally, actions include integrating services within existing healthcare and social systems, reviewing guidelines to remove discriminatory language, and ensuring the use of dignified terminology.
